parole.testo: From Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”, “government”).

parole.significato: forms verbs from adjectives and nouns, equivalent to English -ize
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -ear, from Late Latin -izāre, borrowed from Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō), from Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti, from *-id- + *-yéti. Doublet of -izar, which was borrowed.
Borrowed from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -ear and -ejar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin -mantia, from Ancient Greek μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

Borrowed from Late Latin *abyssimus, from Latin abyssus (“a bottomless gulf”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos, “bottomless”), ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βυσσός (bussós, “depth”). Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese avisso.

parole.significato: acolyte (person ordained to carry the wine, water and lights at Mass)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos).

parole.significato: aphorism (short phrase conveying some principle or concept of thought)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós).
Borrowed from Late Latin anachōrēta, from Ancient Greek ἀναχωρητής (anakhōrētḗs).

parole.significato: anagram (name, word or phrase formed by transposing the letters of another name, word or phrase)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin anagramma, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná) + γράμμα (grámma).

From Old Galician-Portuguese angeo (“angel”), from Late Latin angelus (“angel”), from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”). Cognate with Galician anxo, Spanish ángel, Catalan and Occitan àngel, French ange, Italian angelo and Romanian înger. Doublet of Ângelo and ângelus.

parole.significato: anonymous (wanting a name, not named and determined)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin anōnymus.
From Late Latin apologia, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογία (apología, “a speech in defence”). By surface analysis, apo- + -logia.
Borrowed from Late Latin apologēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós).
From Late Latin poplexia, apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξίᾱ (apoplēxíā), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “to cripple by a stroke”); ἀπο- (apo-, “from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).

parole.significato: apocope (loss or omission of a sound or syllable from the end of a word)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin apocŏpe, from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ), ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin apocryphus (“secret, not approved for public reading”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos, “hidden, obscure”), thus “(books) of unknown authorship”, from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”).

parole.significato: apophasis (allusion to something by denying that it will be mentioned)
parole.testo: Via Late Latin apophasis from Ancient Greek ἀπόφασις (apóphasis, “denial, negation”) from ἀπο- (apo-, “away, from, off”) + φάσις (phásis, “statement, proposition”) from φημί (phēmí, “to speak”) from Proto-Hellenic *pʰā́mā from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂; whence via Proto-Italic *fāōr, *fāmā comes La

From Old Galician-Portuguese apostolo, apostol, borrowed from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “messenger, one sent forth”), from ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to send off”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to set”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese archangeo (“archangel”), semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos).
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”).
From aroma + -ático, from Late Latin arōmata (“spices”), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).

parole.significato: a set practices, such as prayer and meditation, for spiritual enrichment
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ascēsis, from Ancient Greek ἄσκησις (áskēsis, “exercise”).
From Late Latin ascēta, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητής (askētḗs).
From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).

parole.significato: asterisk (symbol used to highlight words or sentences)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk, used in manuscripts to mark passages”).
Borrowed from Late Latin astrologicus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογικός (astrologikós). By surface analysis, astrologia + -ico.
Inherited from Late Latin ballō, from Ancient Greek βαλλίζω (ballízō, “throw”).
Borrowed from Late Latin barytŏnus, from Ancient Greek βαρύτονος (barútonos).
From Late Latin basaltes, a misspelling of Latin basanites, from Ancient Greek βασανίτης (basanítēs), from βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”), from Egyptian bḫn (“a hard stone”) b-x:n-O39
From Old Galician-Portuguese baston, from Late Latin bastum, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “carry”). Doublet of batom.

parole.significato: blasphemous (lacking piety or respect for the sacred)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin blasphēmus, from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”).

parole.significato: common designation, extended to different species of teleost fish from the Sparidae family of seabreams and porgies.
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin bōca, from Ancient Greek βῶκα (bôka), accusative of βῶξ (bôx), a contracted form of βόαξ (bóax), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese bolssa, from Late Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa, “hide”). Doublet of bursa.
Borrowed from Late Latin brūchus.

parole.significato: bronchus (either or two branches of the trachea)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin bronchus, from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos, “trachea, throat”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin būfalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos, “antelope, wild ox”).

From Late Latin cauma (“heat of the midday sun”), from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, especially of the sun”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”). Possibly through the intermediate of Italian calma, although the word was found in Ibero-Romance as early as in Italian.

parole.significato: calvary (representation of the crucifixion of Jesus Christ)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin calvāria (literally “skull”), a calque of Ancient Greek Γολγοθᾶ (Golgothâ), from Aramaic גּוּלְגּוּלְתָּא (gulgultā).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter K/k, called kay in English.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin cappa.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cara, from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cara, from Ancient Greek κάρα (kára, “head, face”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrh₂esn.

parole.significato: phlegm (mucus secreted in the bronchial passages)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos).

parole.significato: catechumen (convert the Christianity prior to baptism)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin catēchūmenus, from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos, “being instructed”), present participle passive of κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to sound through, instruct orally”).

parole.significato: cathedral (relating to the office of a bishop or an archbishop)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρᾱ (kathédrā, “seat”). By surface analysis, cátedra + -al. Piecewise doublet of cadeiral.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin catēgoria, from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).
From Late Latin catēchista, from Ancient Greek κατηχιστής (katēkhistḗs, “oral instructor”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to instruct orally”).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin catēchizāre (“to teach by word of mouth”), from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō, “to instruct orally”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to resound, to instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).

parole.significato: catheter (small tube inserted into a body cavity)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin catheter, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).
From Late Latin catheterismus, from Ancient Greek καθετηρισμός (kathetērismós).
Borrowed from Late Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós, “universal”), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”).

parole.significato: cemetery; graveyard (place where bodies are buried)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion, “sleeping chamber”), from κοιμάω (koimáō, “to put to sleep”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cereija, from Late Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of ceresium, assimilated form of Latin cerasium, borrowed from Ancient Greek κερᾰ́σῐον (kerắsĭon, “cherry (fruit)”), from κερᾰσός (kerăsós) + -ῐον (-ĭon). Cognate with Galician cereixa, Spanish cereza, Ca

Borrowed from Late Latin cyclus (“cycle”), from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”), from Proto-Hellenic *kúklos, *kʷókʷlos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“circle, wheel”). Doublet of chacra.
Inherited from Late Latin zēlōsus (“zealous, jealous”), from zelus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”). Compare the learned borrowing zeloso.
From Late Latin sciaticus, variant of ischiadicus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin clīma, from Ancient Greek κλῐ́μᾰ (klĭ́mă, “region, zone”), from κλῐ́νω (klĭ́nō, “to slope, incline”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese clerigo, crerigo, a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin clēricus, from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós, “(adj. in church jargon) of the clergy”), from κλῆρος (klêros, “the clergy, what is allotted, a lot, inheritance, originally a shard used in casting lots”), from P
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin cuprum (“copper”), from Latin cyprium (aes) (“Cypriot copper”), from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros), because Cyprus was its chief source.
Uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin coccum (“kernel, seed”), from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos). Doublet of coque.

parole.significato: coral (any of various species of anthozoans)
parole.testo: From Late Latin corallum or Latin corallium, from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion, “coral”), of uncertain origin.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cuco, from Late Latin cucus or cuccus, or Latin cuculus or Ancient Greek κόκκυξ (kókkux).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin diaphorēticus, from Ancient Greek διαφορητικός (diaphorētikós).

Borrowed from Late Latin diamantem, from Latin adamantem, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμᾱς (adámās, “invincible, untamed; hard substance”), from ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + δαμάζω (damázō, “to overpower, tame, conquer”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.
Borrowed from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).
Borrowed from Late Latin diūrēticus, from Ancient Greek διουρητικός (diourētikós), from διουρέω (diouréō, “to pass urine, have diuretic properties”).
From Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “an act, a theatrical act, a play”). Doublet of dorama.
From Late Latin drāmaticus, from Ancient Greek δραματικός (dramatikós).
From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι (di) + -πτυχος (-ptukhos) (akin to Greek πτυχή (ptychí, “fold, layer”)).
Borrowed from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós), from ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía).

parole.significato: ecumenical (pertaining to the Christian Church worldwide)
parole.testo: From Late Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos). Compare Italian and Spanish elenco.
From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin entelechīa, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).

Borrowed from Late Latin enthūsiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós, “inspiration, enthusiasm”), from ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: epicycle (a small circle whose centre is on the circumference of a larger circle)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin epicy̆clus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos). By surface analysis, epi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ermo, hermo, from Late Latin eremus, from Latin erēmus, from Ancient Greek ἔρημος (érēmos), with preservation of Greek accent over vowel length in Late Latin. Compare Aromanian ermu
Learned borrowing from Late Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, escândalo + -izar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphēra, from Latin sphaera, borrowed from Ancient Greek σφαῖρᾰ (sphaîră, “ball, globe”).

parole.significato: alms (small amount of money or goods given to someone as charity)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese esmolla, esmolna, earlier elmosna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē).
From Late Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπόρος (spóros, “sowing”) and σπείρω (speírō, “to sow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to strew”).

parole.significato: to evangelize (preach the Christian gospel, especially to non-Christians)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ēvangelizāre, from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).

parole.significato: philanthropy (benevolent altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of mankind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
From Late Latin physiologicus, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογικός (phusiologikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin physiognōmia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμία (phusiognōmía, “physiology”), from φύσις (phúsis, “physique, appearance”) + γνώμη (gnṓmē, “means of knowing”).

parole.significato: phrase (a short written or spoken expression)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

parole.significato: genealogy (the descent of a person, family, or group from an ancestor or ancestors)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin geneālogia, from Ancient Greek γενεᾱλογία (geneālogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin glōssa, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă).
Inherited from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inducing sleep”, “soporific”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hypochondriacus (“pertaining to or affecting the belly”), from Ancient Greek ὑποχονδριακός (hupokhondriakós, “of the region between the ribs and navel”), from ὑποχόνδριος (hupokhóndrios, “the space between the ribs and the navel”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + χόνδρος (khóndro
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos, “river horse”).
From Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ὑφέν (huphén, “together”).

parole.significato: language (form of communication using words and structured with grammar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).

parole.significato: European Portuguese standard spelling of irônico
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehuda, “Judah”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin leopardus from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos) from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “panther”).
Borrowed from Late Latin levisticum, probably an alteration of Latin ligusticum, from Ligusticus (“Ligurian”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Λίγυς (Lígus).

parole.significato: litotes (an understatement employed for rhetoric effect)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs).

From Old Galician-Portuguese lampada, borrowed from Late Latin lampada, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp or flambeau”), from Ancient Greek λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”). Compare the inherited Old Portuguese form lampaa.

parole.significato: logical (in agreement with the principles of logic)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin logicus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
Possibly a derivative of Late Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón).
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). See mania.
From Old Galician-Portuguese melanconia, borrowed from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós).

parole.significato: metonymy (the use of a single characteristic or name of an object to identify the entire object)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).

parole.significato: monogamy (form of relationship in which an individual has only one partner during their lifetime or at any one time)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία (monogamía). By surface analysis, mono- + -gamia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monosyllabicus, from Latin monosyllabus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos). By surface analysis, mono- + silábico.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monasticus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monotonus, from Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos).
Borrowed from Late Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”), from νόσος (nósos, “disease, illness”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of”).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligarca + -ia or oligo- + -arquia
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarquia (“oligarchy”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: onomatopoeia (property of a word of sounding like what it represents)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía, “the coining of a word in imitation of a sound”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodoxo + -ia.

parole.significato: orthodox (adhering to established religious doctrine or tradition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos, “having the right opinion”). By surface analysis, orto- + -doxo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese palavra, with hyperthesis from earlier paravra, paravla, from Late Latin parabola (“speech”), from Latin parabola (“comparison, illustration”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison; parable”). Doublet of parábola, a borrowing.
From Late Latin paradīgma (“paradigm”), from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of palavra. The mathematical sense is taken from New Latin or directly from Greek.
From Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).
From Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).
From Late Latin pasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”). Doublet of espasmo.

parole.significato: dough (mix of flour and other ingredients)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pasta, from Late Latin pasta (“dough, pastry cake, paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá). Cognate with Galician pasta.
From Late Latin pentagōnum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon, “pentagon”), neuter form of πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”). By surface analysis, penta- + -gono.

parole.significato: parchment (writing material made of animal skin)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pergaminho, from Late Latin pergamēna, borrowed from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνὴ (διφθέρα) (Pergamēnḕ (diphthéra), “Pergamene hide”), from Πέργαμον (Pérgamon) + -ηνός (-ēnós). Doublet of pergameno. Compare Galician pergameo and Spanish pergamino.
Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).

parole.significato: plinth (block or slab upon which a column or other structure stands)
parole.testo: From Late Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).

parole.significato: polygamy (the practice of having multiple spouses or partners)
parole.testo: From Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía), itself from πολύγαμος (polúgamos, “married to many”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”). By surface analysis, poli- + -gamia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin polītīa, borrowed from Ancient Greek πολῑτείᾱ (polīteíā), from πολῑ́της (polī́tēs, “citizen”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun–forming suffix).
Borrowed from Late Latin problēmaticus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

From programa (“programme”) + -ção (“-tion”), from Late Latin programma (“a proclamation, edict”), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, “a written public notice, an edict”), from προγράφω (prográphō, “to set forth as a public notice”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).

parole.significato: proselyte (one who has recently converted to a religion or doctrine)
parole.testo: From Late Latin prosēlytus, from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos).

parole.significato: prosthesis (artificial replacement for a body part)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin prothesis, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: chyme (partly digested food passed from the stomach to the duodenum)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin chymus, from Ancient Greek χυμός (khumós, “juice”).
Borrowed from Late Latin rabbi, from Ancient Greek ῥαββί (rhabbí, “rabbi”), from Hebrew רבי (rabbi, “my master”).

parole.significato: to repose; to rest, to relax
parole.testo: From Late Latin repausāre, from Latin re- (“again”) + pausō (“to pause, to rest”), from pausa (“pause”), from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis).

parole.significato: rheumatic (relating to, suffering from or characterised by rheumatism)
parole.testo: From Late Latin rheumaticus, from Ancient Greek ῥευματικός (rheumatikós).

From Old Galician-Portuguese salmo, psalmo, from Late Latin psalmus, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós, “song sung to a harp, performance on a stringed instrument”), from ψάλλω (psállō, “to pluck an instrument”).

Borrowed from Late Latin sarcasmus, from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós, “sneer”), from Ancient Greek σαρκάζειν (sarkázein, “to gnash the teeth”, literally “to tear off the skin”), based on σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).

parole.significato: Semite (member of the Semites, an ethnic group of the Middle East)
parole.testo: From Sem + -ita, from Late Latin Sēm, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from Biblical Hebrew שם (šēm). Compare German Semit, New Latin Sēmīta, French sémite.

parole.significato: mermaid (mythological woman with a fish's tail)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese serẽa, from Late Latin sirēna, from Latin Sīrēn (“siren”), from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). Doublet of sirena and sirene.
From Late Latin sympathīa, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia).
Borrowed from Late Latin syncopāre (“to syncopate (a word)”), from Ancient Greek σύν (sún, “with”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin syntaxis, borrowed from Ancient Greek σῠ́ντᾰξῐς (sŭ́ntăxĭs, “syntax”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sirēna, from Latin Sīrēn (“siren”), from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). Doublet of sereia and sirene.

parole.significato: systematic (belonging to or relating to a system)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin systematicus, from Ancient Greek σῠστημᾰτῐκός (sŭstēmătĭkós). By surface analysis, sistema + -ático.
From Late Latin sȳzygia (“conjunction”), from Ancient Greek συζυγία (suzugía, “union, yoke, pair”).

parole.significato: theory (coherent set of statements attempting to explain observed phenomena)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin theōria (“theory”), from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría, “contemplation; speculation; a looking at; things looked at”), from θεωρέω (theōréō, “to look at, to view, to consider, to examine”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”).

parole.significato: tetrarch (governor of subdivision of a province)
parole.testo: From Late Latin tetrarcha, from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs). By surface analysis, tetra- + -arca.

parole.significato: aunt (sister of someone's father or mother, or an uncle's wife)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese tia, from Late Latin thīa, from Ancient Greek θεία (theía).

parole.significato: uncle (brother of someone's father or mother, or an aunt's husband)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tio, from Late Latin thīus, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Galician and Spanish tío, Italian zio, Sardinian tiu.
From Late Latin tropologicus, from Ancient Greek τροπολογικός (tropologikós). By surface analysis, tropologia + -ico.

parole.significato: trout (fish in Salmonidae which spawns more than once)
parole.testo: From Late Latin tructa, of uncertain origin, possibly from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs). Compare Galician troita.

parole.significato: tomb (small building or vault for the remains of the dead)
parole.testo: From Late Latin tumba (possibly borrowed), from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).

parole.significato: ethics (study of principles governing right and wrong conduct)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), feminine of ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
Inherited from Late Latin orphănus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos.
